query: Consider a homogenized Al0.7CoCrFeNi eutectic alloy initially possessing a dual-phase lamellar structure (FCC/B2) that is strong yet brittle due to stress concentration at incoherent interfaces. The goal is to overcome the strength-ductility trade-off. A hypothesis is proposed involving a High-Pressure and High-Temperature (HPHT) treatment using a hexahedron-anvil apparatus. Predict that applying approximately 6 GPa at 1473 K for 2 hours will induce a topological transformation of the lamellae into a hierarchically patterned microstructure with coherent interfaces. This structure is hypothesized to facilitate multiple deformation mechanisms (dislocation transfer, stacking faults, twinning) and homogeneous strain distribution, effectively arresting interfacial cracking. The mechanism relies on the coherent interface allowing dislocation transfer to alleviate stress. The boundary condition requires that the pressure and temperature are sufficient to induce this specific topological change but not so high as to cause phase instability. A discriminating measurement should compare the fracture surface morphology (isolated microcracks vs. elongated cracks) and the evolution of geometrically necessary dislocation (GND) densities between the treated sample and the baseline, specifically checking if the GND densities of both phases converge at high strain. Falsification would involve showing that conventional thermal-mechanical treatments fail to produce the same hierarchical coherence or GND homogenization.

generation.hypothesis: Applying HPHT treatment (6 GPa, 1473 K, 2 hours) to Al0.7CoCrFeNi eutectic alloy with dual-phase lamellar (FCC/B2) structure will induce a topological transformation into a hierarchically patterned microstructure with coherent interfaces, thereby overcoming the strength-ductility trade-off by enabling multiple deformation mechanisms and homogeneous strain distribution.
generation.material_initial_state: Al0.7CoCrFeNi eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar structure consisting of FCC and B2 phases, exhibiting high strength but brittleness due to stress concentration at incoherent interfaces.
generation.intervention: High-Pressure and High-Temperature (HPHT) treatment using a hexahedron-anvil apparatus at approximately 6 GPa and 1473 K for 2 hours.
generation.conditions: Pressure and temperature must be sufficient to induce topological transformation but not so high as to cause phase instability. Treatment performed in hexahedron-anvil apparatus.
generation.structural_mediator: Hierarchically patterned microstructure with coherent interfaces replacing the original incoherent lamellar interfaces.
generation.mechanism: Coherent interfaces facilitate dislocation transfer between phases, allowing multiple deformation mechanisms (dislocation transfer, stacking faults, twinning) and homogeneous strain distribution, which alleviates stress concentration and arrests interfacial cracking.
generation.predicted_outcome: Enhanced ductility without significant loss of strength, characterized by elongated crack propagation instead of isolated microcracks, and convergence of geometrically necessary dislocation (GND) densities between FCC and B2 phases at high strain.
generation.baseline: As-cast Al0.7CoCrFeNi eutectic alloy with lamellar FCC/B2 structure showing high fracture strength (~944 MPa) and ductility (~25.6% elongation) but limited by incoherent interfaces causing brittleness under certain conditions.
generation.boundary: The treatment parameters (6 GPa, 1473 K, 2 hours) must remain within a window that induces the desired topological transformation without causing phase decomposition or instability.
generation.uncertainty: The exact pressure-temperature window for achieving coherent interfaces without phase instability is not fully established in existing literature. The mechanism of topological transformation under HPHT conditions for this specific alloy composition requires experimental validation. The convergence of GND densities between phases under high strain has not been directly observed in HPHT-treated samples.
generation.falsification_experiment: Conduct conventional thermal-mechanical treatments on Al0.7CoCrFeNi alloy and compare fracture surface morphology and GND density evolution with HPHT-treated samples. If conventional treatments fail to produce hierarchical coherence or GND homogenization, the hypothesis is supported. If HPHT treatment does not result in coherent interfaces or GND convergence, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

To verify this novel alloy design strategy, an industrial scale AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 ingot of ~2.5 kg in weight was prepared, as shown in Fig. 1a . The bulk AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 alloy exhibited an excellent castability with few casting defects, significantly differentiating with other bulk HEAs. The tensile test specimen was machined from the bulk alloy ingot and is shown in Fig. 1b . The cast microstructure of AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 is shown in Fig. 2a . Even in such a bulk cast ingot, a uniform and fine lamellar microstructure characteristic of eutectic alloys was achieved. The inter-lamellar spacing was about 2 μm. The coupled grown two phases showed a clear compositional contrast, with the regions marked by A in Fig. 2b were rich in Co, Cr and Fe, while the regions marked by B were rich in Al and Ni (detailed compositional information given in Table 1 ). An enlarged microstructure given in Fig. 2c shows that dense nanoscale NiAl-rich precipitates (marked as B II ) occurred in the CoCrFe-rich region.
